claims.text: Across 450 transcript-note pairs (12,999 clinical note sentences), an overall hallucination rate of 1.47% was observed.
44% of the identified hallucinations in LLM-generated clinical notes were classified as major clinical risk errors.
Across 49,590 consultation transcript sentences, an overall information omission rate of 3.45% was observed.
16.7% of the identified omissions in LLM-generated clinical notes were classified as major errors.
Incorporating an intermediate atomisation chain-of-thought step to extract facts before generating notes increased major hallucinations and omissions.
Iterative prompt and workflow modifications reduced major errors in LLM clinical note generation below previously reported human note-taking error rates.
Utilizing function call prompts with structured JSON output and enhanced style guidance reduced major omissions from 61 to 0.
Clinician-written notes contained slightly more major hallucinations but fewer omissions compared to LLM-generated notes in Experiment 8.

evidence.description: Of 12,999 sentences in 450 clinical notes, 191 sentences had hallucinations (1.47%).
84 out of 191 hallucinated sentences (44%) were rated as major errors that could impact patient diagnosis and management if left uncorrected.
Of 49,590 transcript sentences, 1,712 sentences were omitted in the summary notes (3.45%).
286 out of 1,712 omitted sentences (16.7%) were classified as major omissions.
Comparing experiment 5 (atomisation) to experiment 3 (structured prompts), major hallucinations increased from 4 to 25 and major omissions increased from 24 to 47.

Experiment 8 achieved 1 major hallucination and 10 major omissions over 25 notes, and Experiment 11 achieved 2 major hallucinations and 0 major omissions, compared to 1 error and 4 omissions reported per human-written note in prior literature.
Across function call iterations from experiment 6 to 11, major omissions decreased from 61 to 0, minor omissions dropped from 130 to 54, and total hallucinations dropped from 4 to 3.
In Experiment 17, clinician-generated notes exhibited slightly more major hallucinations and fewer omissions when evaluated against transcripts compared to Experiment 8 LLM notes.

methodologies.name: CREOLA Clinician-in-the-Loop Framework
methodologies.description: A clinician-in-the-loop clinical evaluation framework and graphical interface incorporating a clinical error taxonomy, experimental pipeline comparison structure, and medical device protocol-inspired clinical safety harm grading.

limitations.text: Automated metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU, and BERTScore fail to capture semantic nuances and contextual dependencies critical for evaluating clinical text quality.
Existing biomedical summarisation benchmarks over scientific literature or radiology reports fail to capture the nuances of direct patient-facing clinical consultation interactions.
The sample size of medical transcripts evaluated per experiment was relatively small (25 transcripts) to balance human annotation workload.
The study evaluated only a single primary language model (GPT-4) with direct prompting structures.
Relying purely on human clinician annotators to manually evaluate generated documentation is expensive and unsustainable at scale.

future_work.text: Apply the CREOLA framework across open-source language models and alternative architectures such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) or knowledge graphs.
Implement scalable automated evaluation via a hybrid 'LLM-as-a-Judge' approach with clinician oversight on sub-samples.
